name: People's Army of Vietnam: people's war in the South (1965-1975)

weightNotes.aggression: Strategic offensives in 1968 (Tet), 1972 (Easter Offensive, 14 divisions and 26 independent regiments) and 1975, but between them main-force units fought only when they chose and withdrew to Laos and Cambodia (Tet, Easter Offensive pages; Pike, PAVN). Moderately high.
weightNotes.maneuver: 1975 was a manoeuvre campaign: Buon Ma Thuot taken on 18 March by a thrust from Cambodia, then forces moved over 350 miles south to Saigon by 30 April (1975 spring offensive page). Earlier, ambush and withdrawal rather than manoeuvre for decision.
weightNotes.flanking: Ambushes and close attacks on landing zones (Ia Drang 1965, where an ambushed US battalion suffered 'a casualty rate of over 50%'); in 1972 assaults were mostly frontal and poorly coordinated (Ia Drang, Easter Offensive pages). Middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Sieges were used to fix and draw in the enemy: Khe Sanh besieged five months in 1968, An Loc in 1972 (Khe Sanh, Easter Offensive pages). Field forces, not towns, were the usual target until 1975. Middling-low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Echeloned forces and strategic reserves held in the North and the sanctuaries; in 1975 the reserve corps were committed only once the ARVN cracked (1975 spring offensive page; Victory in Vietnam, official history). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Detailed reconnaissance and rehearsal before attacks, sapper units, and intelligence from the southern population (People's Army of Vietnam page; Elliott, The Vietnamese War). High.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Easter Offensive 1972: 14 divisions and 26 independent regiments kept attacking and holding (Quang Tri citadel until September) while taking about 100,000 casualties (Easter Offensive page), roughly half the committed force if a division is about 10,000 men (assumption, not on the page). Hue 1968: held the Citadel a little over a month, 1,042-5,133 killed, force size not given (Hue page). Main-force units also broke contact and withdrew when losses mounted (Ia Drang 1965, Dak To 1967), no shares recorded. 0.35, partly derived.
weightNotes.combinedArms: By 1972 tanks (T-54, PT-76), 130 mm guns and SA-7s were fielded, but 'failure of tactical coordination was one of PAVN's prime weaknesses' and almost all armour committed was lost (Easter Offensive page). Better in 1975. 0.45.
weightNotes.initiative: Party control through commissars and front commands, with detailed set-piece plans; regional fronts (B2, Tri-Thien) had latitude, but units executed rehearsed plans rather than improvising (Pike, PAVN; Victory in Vietnam). Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Offensives were timed to stockpiles moved down the Ho Chi Minh Trail by the 559th Group's binh tram stations and trucks (Ho Chi Minh Trail page); the 1972 offensive was 'hampered by high casualties, lack of fuel' when it outran supply (Easter Offensive page). High.

summary: A party-led regular army fighting alongside Viet Cong regional and guerrilla forces under the people's war doctrine: protracted war, with guerrilla, regional and main forces each doing their part, and main-force units committed to conventional offensives when the balance allowed. In the South its regiments and divisions operated from bunker complexes and sanctuaries in Laos and Cambodia, fought close to negate US firepower, and withdrew when losses mounted. Everything was supplied down the Ho Chi Minh Trail. From 1972 it became a conventional combined-arms force with armour, heavy artillery and SAMs.
whyItWorked: Political aims governed military ones: Tet (1968) was a military defeat but turned US opinion and led to negotiations. The trail sustained the war through years of bombing, sanctuaries let units rebuild, and close-in tactics blunted US air and artillery. In 1975 a well-prepared offensive against an ARVN without US air support broke the South between the fall of Buon Ma Thuot (18 March) and Saigon (30 April).
whereItFailed: When it fought conventionally against massed US firepower it lost heavily: the Tet offensive's urban assaults were repelled with very heavy losses and no uprising; the 1972 Easter Offensive cost about 100,000 casualties and almost all its armour (134 T-54s, 56 PT-76s and 60 T-34s) to air power and poor infantry-armour coordination. Khe Sanh (1968) absorbed over 114,000 tons of bombs in three months.

sources.title: Pike, PAVN: People's Army of Vietnam (Presidio, 1986)
